short: China divided between steppe-descended northern regimes and refugee courts in the south.
full:
When the last Eastern Jin emperor was pushed aside in 420, the split that followed lasted almost seventeen decades. In the south, four short dynasties in succession — Song, Qi, Liang and Chen — ruled from Jiankang, modern Nanjing, over an aristocracy descended from families that had fled the north a century earlier. In the north, the Northern Wei, founded by the Xianbei Tuoba clan, had reunified the Yellow River plain by 439 before fracturing in the 530s into rival successor states.

This was not simply a dark age between the Han and the Tang. Emperor Xiaowen moved the Northern Wei capital to Luoyang in 494 and pressed his own nobility to adopt Chinese dress, surnames and language, producing a hybrid northern elite from which the Sui and Tang founders would come. Buddhism spread through both halves under state patronage, leaving the cliff sanctuaries at Yungang and Longmen. The Sui conquest of Chen in 589 ended the division and inherited a country changed by it.
